details.intro: The Life of Adam and Eve narrates the lives of Adam and Eve after their expulsion from Paradise: their penitence, Seth's journey to Paradise for oil from the tree of mercy, Adam's death and burial, and Eve's account of the fall.
details.provenance: The Greek version (often called the Apocalypse of Moses) and the Latin, Armenian, Georgian and Slavonic versions differ widely. The date and origin of the primary Adam literature remain debated: M.D. Johnson (OTP 2) argued for a Jewish original of c. 100 BCE–200 CE, while others regard the work as Christian, of the 2nd–4th c. CE.

details.intro:
The Testament of Adam (TAdam) is a short Christian pseudepigraphon from late antiquity. It was likely composed in Syriac, though it now survives in numerous languages and recensions. In many manuscripts the text is titled ”The testament of our father Adam” or something similar. The document is comprised of two main parts, usually called the Horarium and the Prophecy by modern scholars. The document is conventionally divided into four chapters, with the Horarium comprising the first two chapters and the Prophecy as chapter three. What we often call the fourth chapter is an additional section, the Hierarchy, which only appears in one manuscript and was almost certainly not part of the original document.

The Horarium

In the first main part, the Horarium, Adam lists the hours of the night and/or day in which the various creatures of the creation give praise to God, each in its appointed hour. In most manuscripts this list is divided into two sections, the "Hours of the Night" and the "Hours of the Day," each of which is allotted a chapter in the document's conventional organization. In a few manuscripts, however, one or the other of these sections is missing.

The Greek version of the Horarium seems to have a complex history. The six Greek manuscripts of TAdam contain a modified version of the Horarium that has no connection with Adam. This version is also extant in an Armenian recension. A third, simpler form of the Horarium is found in the work of George Cedrenus (11th century C.E.) where that chronicler describes revelations that Adam received from God. Cedrenus does not provide any other parts of TAdam, though his discussion of Adam's revelations may have been influenced by the Prophecy as well (see below). In any case, the relationship between these three versions of the Horarium (Syriac, Greek, and Cedrenus) is unclear.

The Prophecy

The second part of TAdam, the Prophecy, is a testament with apocalyptic features, presented as the final words of Adam recorded by his son Seth. In it Adam passes on revelations he received from God concerning the future. Some of these revelations concern the relatively near future, focusing on the Flood and Adam's own fate after death. More broadly, Adam describe the eschatological fate his posterity and the world. The Christian nature of the document is most visible when Adam predicts the divine incarnation. 

The Hierarchy

One late manuscript (Vatican Syr 164, 1702 C.E.) appends a unique section concerning the heavenly orders, with the heading ”Also from the testament of our father Adam." This section, usually designated the Hierarchy, is an angelology which lists the nine orders of the heavenly beings and their functions. Since it only appears in one manuscript, and since its content is incompatible with the narrative fiction of the two other parts, the Hierarchy was probably not part of the original TAdam. Nevertheless, modern scholars often include it as a fourth chapter of the document.
details.provenance:
A Syriac Christian Document

Beginning with M. E. Renan, the Testament of Adam was long regarded by modern scholars as a Gnostic work, but both Reinink and Robinson have shown this view to be wrong. Robinson has argued that the Syriac recension 1 is likely the most ancient form of TAdam known to us, and he has furnished good evidence that the original language of both the Horarium and the Prophecy was Syriac (Robinson, 137-42). If Robinson is correct, the work in its present form most likely originated within the Christian communities of Syria in late antiquity.

Earlier Jewish Sources?

The question of earlier sources is closely related to the question of unity. In all its extant forms the Horarium and the Prophecy are presented together as a unified composition, and their redactional and compositional history is difficult to untangle with any certainty. Still, the two parts are strikingly different in form and genre. Various literary elements also strongly suggest that the Horarium and the Prophecy were once two separate documents, combined and adapted at some point by a redactor to produce the Christian work we know.

The original Horarium would then likely have been a Jewish work, not necessarily related to Adam at all. The Prophecy could very well have been a Christian work from the beginning, but it could also be a heavily redacted Jewish composition. On the basis of a passage from the Apocalypse of Elijah (???), Robinson tentatively suggests that this earlier version of the Prophecy was composed in the third century C.E. and the earlier independent Horarium no later than that (Robinson, 150–3). Richard Bauckham has since made the case that the Horarium originated as a Jewish work from the second temple period (Bauckham, 2002).

The Provenance of the Hierarchy

The Hierarchy has only been superficially adapted to fit TAdam. The speaker, supposed to be Adam, refers to biblical events in past time and addresses ”my beloved” (plural; 4:1). The Hierarchy might well be a lightly redacted version of a Jewish angelology, possibly dating from the Second Temple period. The Christian additions may have involved nothing more than the interpolation of ”Jesus Christ” into 4:1 and 4:8 (see Robinson, 146-48; 159-60).
details.manuscripts:
Syriac Text

The earliest form of the Testament of Adam is witnessed in eight manuscripts dating between the 9th and the 18th centuries C.E.  The Syriac manuscripts are divided into three recensions based on content, chronology, writing system and arrangement of the four sections. (Note that the dating and alphabetic names for these manuscripts are all taken from S.E. Robinson's The Testament of Adam: An Examination of the Syriac and Greek Traditions. SBLDS 52; Chico, Ca.: Scholars Press, 1982.)

Recension 1

Recension 1 consists of the aforementioned Manuscript A (BM Add. 14,624 [folios 8b-10a]), dating to the early 9th century B.C.E., in addition to Manuscript B (Vat. Syr. 58), which is and dated to the late 16th century. Manuscript A is written in the Estrangela script with some letters in Serta, while Manuscript B is written entirely in Serta. Both manuscripts contain the Horarium (Hours of the Night and Hours of the Day) and the Prophecy in that order. In spite of the chronological differences, these two mss are nearly identical in content.

Recension 2

Recension 2 consists of Manuscript C (Vat. Syr. 164), written in Nestorian and dated to the early 18th century, and Manuscript D (BM Add 25,875), also written in Nestorian and dated to the early 18th century. Manuscript C contains the Horarium (only the Hours of the Night), the Prophecy and – as the sole witness – the Hierarchy. Manuscript D contains only the Prophecy.

Recension 3

Recension 3 consists of the following manuscripts: Manuscript E (Arund. Or. 53), written in Serta and dated to the 16th century, Manuscript F (Vat. Syr 159) written in Serta and dated to the 17th century, Manuscript G (Rylands 44) written in Nestorian and dated to the 15th century and Manuscript H (BM Add 14,577), written in Estrangela and dated to the late 9th century. All manuscripts in Recension 3 contain the Horarium except in the same order as the Greek versions, with the Hours of the Day first, followed by the Hours of the Night. Manuscripts E and H merely contain the Horarium. Manuscript F is the only one in Recension 3 that contains the Prophecy. Manuscript G also contains the so-called Treatise of Shem.

Greek Text

The Greek version of TAdam comes to us in two independent forms. Both contain only the Horarium. One recension is witnessed in six Greek manuscripts from the 15th to the 17th centuries C.E. This modified version of the Horarium bears no connection with Adam or with a testamentary context. It seems to be a late reworking of the Syriac recension 3, in part because it reverses the order of the Hours of the Night and Hours of the Day in the same way. This Greek recension bears some resemblance to late Byzantine magical texts and in most cases appears as part of a larger work on astrology and magic called Apotelesmata, attributed in some of the manuscripts to Apollonius of Tyana. This peculiar magic-Apollonius version of the Horarium is also extant in Armenian (published in Stone, pp. 39-77).

The other form of the Greek Horarium appears in one passage from Cedrenus. Here the 11th century chronicler lists the hours of the day in which prayers are sent up to heaven. Again this list is not attached to a version of the Prophecy, and it does not appear in a testamentary context. Unlike the other Greek witnesses, however, Cedrenus does connect this modified Horarium with Adam, presenting it among the revelations Adam received from God. Although Cedrenus only lists the hours of the day, the chronicler tells us that both the hours of the day and the hours of the night had been revealed to Adam. An almost verbatim passage in George Syncellus (9th century) is likely the Vorlage for Cedrenus' Horarium. Unfortunately the text of Syncellus is damaged from the point where the listing of the hours would begin.

* **Date and Context**: Copied ca. mid-4th century CE; the Greek original is widely dated between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. Strikingly, the work lacks explicit Christian terminology or overt references to Jesus Christ, making it central to debates over non-Christian Jewish-Gnostic apocalypticism and Sethian origins.

details.intro: 1 Enoch is a collection of five Enochic works: the Book of the Watchers (1–36), the Similitudes (37–71), the Astronomical Book (72–82), the Book of Dreams (83–90) and the Epistle of Enoch (91–108). It deals with the fall of the watchers, cosmic geography and the calendar, and the final judgment.
details.provenance: The oldest parts date from the 3rd–2nd c. BCE; the Similitudes are probably from the 1st c. CE. Aramaic fragments of every part except the Similitudes were found at Qumran. The complete work survives only in Ge'ez; substantial portions survive in Greek.

The *Liber Antiquitatum Biblicarum* (commonly abbreviated *LAB*, also known as *Pseudo-Philo* or *Biblical Antiquities*) is one of the most substantial and significant works of Second Temple Jewish literature. Spanning sixty-five chapters, the work is a monumental "Rewritten Bible" narrative recounting sacred history from Adam to the tragic death of King Saul. details.intro:
4 Ezra was originally composed as a pseudepigraphal Jewish apocalypse, most likely in Hebrew, at some point after 70 CE (see discussion below).

The original Hebrew version, which is now lost, was translated into Greek. The Greek version, which survives only in fragmentary quotations and paraphrases by later Christian authors, was translated into Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Georgian, Arabic, Armenian and Coptic. Additional translations from the Latin and Syriac versions also exist (Stone, 4 Ezra, 2). The apocalypse takes the name, 4 Ezra, from the Latin version, which was labeled 4 Esdras to distinguish it from 1 Esdras (=Ezra), 2 Esdras (=Nehemiah), and 3 Esdras (the apocryphal book now normally designated 1 Esdras). To make matters more complicated, 4 Ezra is often called 2 Esdras by modern English translations, such as the KJV, RSV and NRSV, that adopt the traditional Hebrew names for Ezra and Nehemiah and include the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras. The Latin version included as an appendix to the Vulgate was transformed into a Christian text by the addition of an introduction (chapters 1-2) and conclusion (chapters 15-16), commonly designated 5th and 6th Ezra by modern scholars. Most modern English translations follow the Vulgate in printing the Christian 5th and 6th Ezra along with the Jewish apocalypse of 4 Ezra. As a result, the chapter and verse numbering of the apocalypse begin at chapter 3 verse 1.
details.provenance:
Date

Terminus ante quem

The earliest definite quotation from 4 Ezra occurs in Clement of Alexandria’s Stromateis. Since Stromateis is dated to the end of the 2nd century CE, 4 Ezra must have been written and translated into Greek no later than the end of the 2nd century. If the possible reference in Barnabas 12:1 is accepted as a quotation, 4 Ezra will have been composed by the end of the first century.

4 Ezra is also closely related to 2 Baruch, which is normally dated to the end of the first or the beginning of the second century, but the precise date of 2 Baruch is uncertain, and the nature of the relationship between the two documents remains disputed. (See the introduction to 2 Baruch for more discussion.)

Terminus post quem

4 Ezra’s preoccupation with the destruction of Jerusalem indicates that the book was composed after 70 CE, but near enough to the event still to raise deep theological questions. If the “three heads” in Ezra’s eagle vision (12:22-28), that appear immediately before a description of the “end” (12:29-36), are coded references to Vespasian and his two sons Titus and Domitian, the book will have been composed during the reign of Domitian (81-96 CE). This corresponds to the reference to “the thirtieth year after the destruction of the city” in 3:1, although this date may simply recall Ezek 1:1 (cf. Stone, 4 Ezra, 9-10; Schürer III.1, 299-300).

Original Language

Although L. Gry argued that 4 Ezra was originally composed in Aramaic, most recent scholars agree with Wellhausen, Gunkel and, more recently, Klijn, that the original language was Hebrew (Schürer III.1, 300; Stone, 4 Ezra, 10-11; Metzger, “4 Ezra,” 519-520).

The *Words of Ahiqar* is one of the most ancient and widely dispersed wisdom and narrative cycles of the ancient Near East and Mediterranean world. It comprises two distinct literary components:
1. **The Narrative Frame**: The biographical account of Ahiqar, wise chancellor (*ummânu*) and keeper of the signet to Sennacherib and Esarhaddon of Assyria; his betrayal by his adopted nephew/pupil Nadan; his secret preservation by the executioner Nabusumiskun; and his triumphant restoration when he solves the impossible architectural and riddle contests posed by the Pharaoh of Egypt.
2. **The Sayings and Fables**: An extensive collection of instructional wisdom sayings, proverbs, and beast fables addressed by Ahiqar to Nadan.

details.intro: *4 Maccabees* (Μακκαβαίων Δʹ / *Liber IV Maccabaeorum*; titled in patristic antiquity Περὶ αὐτοκράτορος λογισμοῦ, *On the Sovereignty of Reason*) is a masterpiece of Hellenistic Jewish philosophical rhetoric. Cast in the form of a formal Greek diatribe or epideictic encomium, the work synthesizes Stoic and Platonic philosophical ethics with strict devotion to the Mosaic Torah. The author sets out to demonstrate a singular philosophical thesis: that *pious reason* (*ho eusebēs logismos*) exercises absolute mastery over the emotions and passions (*autokratōr estin tōn pathōn*). To establish this proposition, the author presents the heroic martyrdoms of the aged priest Eleazar, the seven young brothers, and their mother under the Seleucid tyrant Antiochus IV Epiphanes (expanding and dramatically reinterpreting the narrative of 2 Maccabees 6:18–7:42).

details.intro: The *Odes of Solomon* (Syriac: *Zmīrāthā d-Shlēmūn*; Greek: Ὠιδαὶ Σολομῶντος / *Ōidai Solomōntos*; Latin: *Odae Salomonis*) is a collection of forty-two ecstatic lyrical hymns (Odes 1–42; Ode 2 is lost due to a physical lacuna in the manuscript traditions). Composed around the late 1st or early 2nd century CE (ca. 100–125 CE) in Roman Syria (most likely Antioch or Edessa/Osrhoene), the *Odes* constitute the earliest surviving Christian hymnal. Imbued with profound mystical intimacy, realized eschatology, and poetic passion, the collection reflects a bilingual Semitic-Hellenistic milieu that bridges the theological world of the Dead Sea Scrolls (*Hodayot*), the Gospel of John, and the letters of Saint Ignatius of Antioch.

details.intro: The Testament of Job retells the story of Job as a deathbed address to his children. Job destroys an idol's temple, is attacked by Satan in return, and endures with patience until Satan concedes defeat. The kings who visit him, the death of his wife Sitis, and the heavenly sashes he gives his daughters, who then speak in angelic tongues, are distinctive features.
details.provenance:
Original Language

The Testament of Job was most likely composed in Greek (so Spittler, 830, 833). It shows no obvious signs of being translated from a semitic language, and no evidence has been found of versions in Hebrew, Aramaic, or Syriac.

Date of Composition

The Testament of Job was composed some time prior to the 5th century CE, when the earliest surviving fragments were copied. Since that 5th century evidence preserves a Coptic translation, the original Greek composition would probably have been made at least several decades earlier. It may have been composed in the first century BCE or first century CE (so Spittler, 833).

Social Setting

The Testament of Job has generally been viewed as a Jewish composition, free in its present form from any extensive Christian editing (Spittler, 833-34; see Brock, 8). James Davila has recently dissented from this consensus and argued that the document is a Christian composition, or at least that an origin in early Christian circles cannot be ruled out.

The transcription of V published by Mai in 1833 (see below) was the first publication of the Testament of Job. Mai's edition is reasonably accurate, but not without significant errors. This ms has not been published since in running form, and the partial transcription by F. C. Conybeare in 1901 (see below) is less accurate than that of Mai. Manuscript V is closer to S in the form of its text than to P, so that S and V appear to represent a common textual trajectory distinct from that represented in P (Brock, 14; Kraft, 9-10). Nevertheless, V does not appear to be directly dependent on ms S. V is generally agreed to depart further than P or S from the early form of the Greek text, and it includes many periphrastic expansions (Brock, 9; Kraft, 5).

Many of its periphrastic expansions parallel the kind of editorial work evident in ms V. Nevertheless, the Slavonic tradition is not clearly derived from either the P or the S V textual traditions, but seems to translate a Vorlage which included readings characteristic of both streams of textual transmission (Brock, 14-15).

details.intro:
The Psalms of Solomon (PssSol) is a Jewish pseudepigraphical collection of eighteen poetic psalms composed in Judea during the turbulent midpoint of the first century BCE (ca. 63–37 BCE) and brought into its final composite form prior to the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE. Pseudepigraphically attributed to King Solomon—celebrated in biblical tradition for his wisdom, proverbs, and thousands of songs (cf. 1 Kgs 4:32; canonical Ps 72)—the collection captures the acute communal trauma, factional conflict, and fervent eschatological longings of Jewish society following the collapse of Hasmonean sovereignty and the Roman conquest of Jerusalem by Pompey the Great in 63 BCE.

Although not preserved in the canonical Hebrew Bible or among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Psalms of Solomon was faithfully transmitted through Christian ecclesiastical channels in the Greek East. Ancient canonical catalogues—most notably the fifth-century table of contents (Pinax) of Codex Alexandrinus (which lists the eighteen psalms among the antilegomena following 1–2 Clement), the sixth-century Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae (pseudo-Athanasius), and the ninth-century Stichometry of Nicephorus (which measures the work at 2,100 stichoi)—demonstrate that the collection was read and copied as a significant ecclesiastical appendix to Septuagint and New Testament codices.

Spanning an array of classical biblical poetic genres, the collection includes communal laments (PssSol 1, 2, 8), individual prayers of thanksgiving and penitence (PssSol 3, 5, 6, 9, 13, 15, 16), wisdom and didactic reflections (PssSol 4, 10, 14), and royal messianic hymns (PssSol 17, 18). It stands alongside the Dead Sea Scrolls as one of the most vital textual witnesses to late Second Temple Palestinian Jewish theology, articulating a profound theodicy in the face of foreign subjugation, an acute ethical dualism between the "righteous" and "sinners," an explicit hope in the bodily resurrection of the righteous to eternal life, and the most detailed pre-Christian portrait of a personal, Davidic Messiah (huios Dauid) in ancient Jewish literature.
details.provenance:
Date and Historical Setting

The historical backdrop of the Psalms of Solomon is anchored in the dramatic political convulsions of first-century BCE Judea. Three psalms in particular—2, 8, and 17—contain vivid, transparent historical allusions that allow modern scholars to date their composition with remarkable precision:

  • The Siege and Fall of Jerusalem (63 BCE): Psalm 8 recounts the approach of a foreign conqueror from the ends of the earth who was welcomed by the city's corrupt leadership, assaulted the fortified walls with battering rams (8:15–21; cf. 2:1), and desecrated the Temple sanctuary, trampling the holy altar with pagan feet (2:2). As first recognized by F. K. Movers in the nineteenth century, this corresponds exactly to the Roman siege led by Pompey the Great in 63 BCE, intervening in the civil war between the Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II as recounted by Flavius Josephus (Ant. 14.3–4; J.W. 1.6–7).
  • The Denunciation of Late Hasmonean Usurpation: The psalms deliver a scathing theological polemic against the native Hasmonean priest-kings (Aristobulus II, Hyrcanus II, and Alexander Jannaeus). The psalmist charges them with unlawfully arrogating royal majesty to themselves without Davidic covenantal legitimacy (17:5–8) and defiling the altar, sanctuary, and sacrificial rites with ritual impurity and incest (8:11–13, 22; 2:3–14). The Roman assault is thus interpreted not as a tragic defeat of God's people, but as a deserved divine punishment upon an apostate aristocracy.
  • The Ignominious Fate of Pompey (48 BCE): Psalm 2:26–27 provides a decisive terminus post quem for the collection, describing the dishonorable end of the Roman conqueror: "I did not have to wait long before God showed me the insolent one lying dead on the mountains of Egypt, despised more than the smallest on land and sea, his body decomposed by the waves with no one to bury him." This matches Pompey's assassination on the beach of Pelusium in Egypt in 48 BCE following his defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus, where his headless body was left exposed on the shore.
  • Herod the Great's Siege and the Atkinson Redating Thesis: While earlier scholars (e.g., Ewald, Bretschneider, Cellier) proposed obsolete dates ranging from Ptolemy I to Titus, Kenneth Atkinson ("Toward a Redating of the Psalms of Solomon," 1998; "Herod the Great, Sosius, and the Siege of Jerusalem," 1996) argues that Psalm 17 reflects the bloody siege of Jerusalem in 37/36 BCE by Herod the Great and the Roman general Gaius Sosius. Atkinson suggests that the collection spans the historical transition from the late Hasmonean period to the early Herodian era (ca. 63–30 BCE), reflecting an ongoing community that weathered both crises.

The complete absence of any allusion to the cataclysmic destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE firmly establishes that the collection attained its final redacted form before 70 CE, with the majority of psalms composed between 63 and 40 BCE (as proposed by R. B. Wright, E. P. Sanders, and M. de Jonge).

Authorship, Provenance, and Sectarian Milieu

The collection was composed in Judea, almost certainly in Jerusalem or its immediate environs. The identity of the community behind the psalms has been one of the most vigorously debated problems in Second Temple scholarship:

  • The Pharisaic Hypothesis: Pioneered by Julius Wellhausen (Die Pharisäer und die Sadducäer, 1874) and popularized by H. E. Ryle and M. R. James in their landmark edition Psalms of the Pharisees, Commonly Called the Psalms of Solomon (1891), this view held that the authors were Pharisees opposing the Sadducean Hasmonean hierarchy. The thesis was supported by the poems' fierce devotion to Torah, belief in divine sovereignty alongside human free will, insistence on bodily resurrection, and strict purity regulations. Mikael Winninge (Sinners and the Righteous, 1995) has defended a modified version of this stance.
  • The Post-Qumran Critique: The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls decisively shattered the exclusivity of the Pharisaic identification. As demonstrated by J. O'Dell (1961) and R. B. Wright (1972), doctrines such as divine retribution, bodily resurrection, messianic deliverance, and hatred for Hasmonean corruption were not distinctive to Pharisees, but were widely shared across the broader apocalyptic and pietistic streams of Palestinian Judaism. The internal evidence proves firmly that the authors were non-Sadducean, but does not identify them uniquely as Pharisees.
  • The Essene and Qumran-Adjacent Hypotheses: André Dupont-Sommer (1973) proposed that the psalms originated among the Essenes, a hypothesis further refined by P. N. Franklyn (1987), who posited a previously unrecorded branch of the Essene movement. However, no copies or fragments of the Psalms of Solomon have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the references to fleeing into the wilderness (PsSol 17:16) reflect temporary flight during siege warfare rather than permanent communal withdrawal to Qumran.
  • The Zadokite Displacement Model: Advanced by Heerak Christian Kim (Zadokite Propaganda in the Late Second Temple Period, 2014), this theory links the collection with displaced Oniad/Zadokite priests who were ousted from the Temple cult by the Hasmoneans and who produced polemical psalms protesting their disenfranchisement and calling for cultic restoration.
  • The Modern Consensus: Unknown Jerusalem Pietists: The dominant contemporary perspective, articulated by Kenneth Atkinson (I Cried to the Lord, 2004) and endorsed by E. P. Sanders, concludes that the authors cannot be identified with any known historical sect (Pharisees, Sadducees, or Essenes). Rather, the psalms were composed by an unknown, pietistic Jerusalem circle—self-designated as "the assemblies of the devout" (συναγωγαὶ ὁσίων, PsSol 17:16)—rooted in traditional Hasidic piety (Büchler 1922; Flusser 1984; Hann 1988) and maintaining strict covenantal fidelity amid socio-political marginalization.

Original Language and Translation Character

The overwhelming majority of modern scholars (including Ryle and James, G. B. Gray, Emil Schürer, Joseph L. Trafton, and Robert B. Wright) maintain that the Psalms of Solomon was originally composed in Hebrew, and subsequently translated into Greek, from which the Syriac version later derived (or, as Trafton and Grant Ward argue, with both versions reflecting independent access to a common Hebrew Vorlage). The case for a lost Hebrew original rests on several converging lines of philological evidence:

  • Pervasive Semitic Syntax: The Greek text exhibits continuous coordinate clauses linked by καί, construct-state periphrases, rigid Hebrew word order, and idioms that represent word-for-word calques of classical biblical Hebrew poetry.
  • Demonstrable Translation Errors: Several obscure or impossible Greek readings are explicable only as misreadings or graphic confusion of Hebrew consonants. For example, at PsSol 2:25, the translator appears to have misread Hebrew rymhl ("to change/alter") as rm'l ("to say"), producing the ungrammatical Greek phrase τοῦ εἰπεῖν. Similarly, at PsSol 2:26, the description of Pompey's insolence (ἡ ὑπερηφανία αὐτοῦ) likely reflects a graphic confusion of Hebrew g'wtw ("his pride") for gwytw ("his corpse").
  • Intertextual Dependence with Baruch: The undeniable literary relationship between Psalm of Solomon 11 and Baruch 5:5–8 demonstrates that one work drew upon the other. Because PsSol 11 displays superior poetic unity and structural cohesion, scholars widely judge that Baruch translated or adapted a pre-existing Hebrew Vorlage of Psalm 11.
  • The Syriac Evidence: Comprehensive philological analysis by Joseph L. Trafton (1985, 1986) indicates that while the Syriac text shows close affinity with the Greek manuscript family of Group 253, several Syriac readings preserve genuine Semitic idioms or variants that suggest access to a Semitic Vorlage.

A vocal minority (beginning with Hilgenfeld in 1871 and revisited by some contemporary linguists) has argued for direct Greek composition in intentional imitation of the Septuagint. However, as Kenneth Atkinson notes in the NETS commentary, the persistent "lexical stereotyping" (e.g., translating Hebrew hasid uniformly as ὅσιος and hesed as ἔλεος) and syntactical stiffness are standard hallmarks of translation Greek rather than Hellenistic Greek composition.
details.manuscripts:
The Greek Manuscript Tradition

The Greek text of the Psalms of Solomon survives in eleven manuscripts dating from the tenth to the sixteenth century CE. Through the stemmatic analyses of Robert R. Hann (The Manuscript History of the Psalms of Solomon, 1982), Robert B. Wright (The Psalms of Solomon: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text, 2007), and Felix Albrecht (Göttingen Septuagint XII,3, 2018), these witnesses are classified into four distinct textual families, alongside ancient indirect witnesses:

Ancient Indirect Attestation

  • Codex Alexandrinus (MS A, 5th century CE): Listed in the table of contents (Pinax) under disputed books (antilegomena) immediately following 1–2 Clement with the entry ΨΑΛΜΟΙ ΣΟΛΟΜΩΝΤΟΣ ΙΗ ("Eighteen Psalms of Solomon"). The folios containing the text at the very end of the great codex were lost prior to the modern era, but the entry proves its canonical reception in late antique Egypt.
  • Patristic Stichometries: Cited in the pseudo-Athanasian Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae (early 6th c.) and the Stichometry of Nicephorus (Patriarch of Constantinople, 9th c.), which reckons the work at 2,100 stichoi among the ecclesiastical books.

The Syriac Tradition

The Psalms of Solomon is also preserved in the Syriac tradition across five manuscripts (critical edition by W. Baars, 1972):

  • MS S (7th century CE): A fragmentary marginal text preserved in the margin of a manuscript of the Hymns of Severus of Antioch (British Library, Add. 14538).
  • The Complete Syriac Codices: Manchester, John Rylands Library, Syr. 9 (the celebrated 16th-century "Harris codex"); Birmingham, Selly Oak Colleges, Mingana Syr. 163; Cambridge, University Library, Add. 2012; and Jerusalem, St. Mark's Monastery, Syr. 161.

In the Syriac manuscripts, the eighteen psalms are appended directly to the Odes of Solomon, numbered continuously as Odes 43–60. Philological evaluations by Joseph L. Trafton (1985) demonstrate that the Syriac translation differs from the Greek in only about 62 verses (roughly 10%) and shows an intimate affinity with the Greek archetype of Group 253, while in several passages reflecting independent Semitic idioms.

History of Printed Editions

  • Editio Princeps (1626): First printed by the Jesuit scholar Juan Luis de la Cerda in his Adversaria Sacra (Lyon, 1626), based on a transcript of MS 149 rediscovered in Augsburg by David Hoeschel (1556–1617).
  • Oscar von Gebhardt (1895): Die Psalmen Salomo’s; the foundation of modern stemmatic criticism, expanding the known Greek witnesses from five to eight manuscripts through Mount Athos discoveries.
  • Alfred Rahlfs (1935): Septuaginta; incorporated eight manuscripts, providing the widely adopted standard chapter and verse numbering.
  • Robert B. Wright (2007): The Psalms of Solomon: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text; the first complete edition to collate all eleven Greek manuscripts and four Syriac codices with high-resolution digital imaging.
  • Felix Albrecht (2018): Psalmi Salomonis (Göttingen Septuagint XII,3); the definitive monumental edition providing exhaustive stemmatic apparatus, patristic citations, and orthographic documentation.

details.intro: The *Lives of the Prophets* (Greek: Περὶ τῶν βίων καὶ τῆς τελευτῆς τῶν προφητῶν / *Peri tōn biōn kai tēs teleutēs tōn prophētōn*; Latin: *Vitae prophetarum* / *De vitis prophetarum*; Syriac: *Tash'yāthā d-nebīyē*) is an ancient Jewish hagiographical and biographical compendium detailing the careers, origins, ancestral tribes, prophetic signs, deaths, martyrdoms, and burial locations of twenty-three biblical prophets. Attributed spuriously in early Christian transmission to **Epiphanius of Salamis** (Cyprus, 4th c.) or **Dorotheus of Tyre**, the core document is a product of 1st-century CE Palestinian Judaism, compiled in Greek (or translated very early from Hebrew) prior to the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple in 70 CE.

details.intro: Most scholars conclude the Apocalypse of Baruch (2 Baruch) is a Jewish composition from the regions in or around Judea, written around the end of the first century CE (see discussion below).
details.provenance:
Date

2 Baruch is a pseudepigraphal work written from the perspective of Baruch, the scribe of Jeremiah, and set around the time of the destruction of Solomon's Temple in 586 BCE. However, it is clear that 2 Baruch presupposes the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE (cf. 32.2-4), and that the author was primarily concerned with the theological and pastoral implications of the destruction of the Second Temple. Nickelsburg rightly indicates that the author of 2 Baruch is still "deeply grieved by the events of the year 70" (Jewish Literature, 283).

It is more difficult to determine when, after 70 CE, 2 Baruch was written. The vague reference in 28.2 to the ‘calculation of time in two parts’ pertaining to ‘weeks of seven weeks’ is too vague to be of much value (see L. Gry, “Date de la fin des temps, scion les révélations ou les calcula du Pseudo-Philo et de Baruch [Apocalypse syriaque],” RB 48 [1939]: 337-56). There is also an affinity between 2 Baruch 61.7 and Barnabas 11.9 (written between 117 and 132 CE?), though this may be due to both authors' use of a common source.

Another factor relevant to the dating of 2 Baruch is the document's evidently close relationship with 4 Ezra. Unfortunately, the date of 4 Ezra is itself uncertain (see G. H. Box, “IV Ezra,” APOT 2.553-54). Moreover, while interdependence between the two documents is almost certain, the nature, extent, and order of this interdependence is disputed (Nickelsburg). Although 2 Baruch and 4 Ezra share significant overlaps in content, there are broad thematic differences in their treatment of this common material. Whereas 4 Ezra educes a careful theodicy in response to the tragedy of the temple's destruction, the concerns evident in 2 Baruch are more “pastoral and practical,” addressing matters of consolation and exhortations toward reconstruction (Nickelsburg, Jewish Literature, 283). This ambiguous situation has produced four main suggestions over the past century as to the (inter)relationship of the two apocalypses:

  1. 4 Ezra was dependent on 2 Baruch (see list on Bogaert, L'Apocalypse, 1.26);
  2. 2 Baruch was dependent on 4 Ezra (see list on Bogaert, L'Apocalypse, 1.26; Box, APOT 2:553; Metzger, OTP 2:522);
  3. both were dependent on a common source (Klijn, Arabic Text, 620);
  4. we cannot determine the direction of the dependence (Charles, APOT 2:477; Michael E. Stone, Fourth Ezra [Minneapolis : Fortress Press, 1990], 39).

For a complete, updated discussion, see Nickelsburg, Jewish Literature, 283-85 and see the bibliography below for research between 1999 and 2006.

Some would see this cumulative, though tenuous, evidence to point to a date for 2 Baruch in the first or second decade of the second century CE (Klijn, Arabic Text, 617). Others argue that the document was written toward the end of the first century (Nickelsburg, Jewish Literature, 283), perhaps in 96 CE specifically (Bogaert, L'Apocalypse, 1.294-95; cf. also Nicolae Roddy, “‘Two Parts: Weeks of Seven Weeks’: The End of the Age as Teminus ad Quem for 2 Baruch,” JSP 14 [1996] 3–14).

Locale

2 Baruch was probably written in Judea, Galilee, or a neighbouring region. The original language of the document was most likely Hebrew or Aramaic, and the work shows affinities with later rabbinic literature originating from the land of Israel (Klijn, Arabic Text, 617). The author of 2 Bar. also seems to identify himself with the inhabitants of Palestine who have survived the Roman onslaught, and it is from this standpoint that he exhorts the Jews of the Diaspora in the epistle (Klijn, Arabic Text, 617).

Cultural and Historical Context

According to J. E. Wright, “The overall goal of 2 Baruch is to promote obedience to God’s commandments as the way to survive in difficult times” (“Baruch, Books of,” DNTB, 148-151). The book, somewhat like 4 Ezra, is the author’s attempt both to make theological sense of the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, and to exhort Israel to remain faithful to her God in hope of restoration. It is widely agreed that 2 Bar. was originally composed in non-Christian Jewish circles, and the contention that it is instead a Christian composition (Nir, Destruction of Jerusalem, passim) has not found much support. Nonetheless, 2 Bar. is a "Christian text" in the sense that it was adopted and preserved within Christian circles for much of its transmission history.

details.intro: *2 Baruch* (the *Syriac Apocalypse of Baruch*) is a premier Jewish apocalypse composed in Judea around the end of the 1st century or early 2nd century CE (ca. 95–110 CE), in the tragic aftermath of the Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE. Written in a Hebrew or Aramaic original that was translated into Greek, the complete text has survived only in a single Syriac manuscript (along with an Arabic version discovered in 1975).

details.intro: 3 Baruch (the Greek Apocalypse of Baruch) describes Baruch, grieving over the destruction of Jerusalem, being led by an angel through five heavens. There he sees the punishment of the tower-builders, the dragon of Hades, the sun and moon, and Michael receiving the prayers of the righteous.
details.provenance: It survives in Greek and Slavonic. A Jewish work of the 1st–2nd c. CE with Christian revision is the common view, though some regard it as Christian.

details.intro: The Letter of Aristeas describes how Demetrius of Phalerum persuaded Ptolemy II to have the Jewish law translated into Greek. Seventy-two elders come from Jerusalem, answer the king's questions at banquets, and complete the translation, which the Alexandrian Jewish community then approves.
details.provenance: Written in Greek by an Alexandrian Jew, the letter is generally dated to the 2nd c. BCE. It was transmitted in Greek manuscripts of the catenae on the Octateuch.

details.intro: The Sibylline Oracles are quoted extensively by the church fathers (see Thompson, “Patristic Use of the Sibylline Oracles,” Review of Religion [1952] 115-36). They also influenced Renaissance literature and art.
details.provenance:
Though the Jewish and Christian oracles contained in this collection are the only extant extended versions of the genre to survive, oracles of the Sibyl were extremely popular in Greco-Roman antiquity from the 5th century BCE onward. The Sibyl, characterized as an aged female prophetess whose “raving mouth” (Plutarch, Moralia 397A) almost always forecasted doom, uttered her oracles in Greek hexameter and her oracles usually served purposes of political propaganda. Caesar Augustus is said to have destroyed two thousand prophetic books, including some Sibylline Oracles, because of their subversive nature (Seutonius, Augustus 31:1). The earliest Sibyl was believed to have lived in Erythea in Ionia. Other well known Sibyls are associated with Cumae in Italy and Marpessus in Asia Minor (Collins 1983: 317). The proliferation of Sibyls led to various attempts to enumerate them. The most influential of these lists was that of Varro, who counted ten (Lactantius DivInst.1.6). The prologue of the present collection repeats this list but associates the Persian Sibyl with an otherwise unknown Hebrew Sibyl.

If, as is widely argued (see below), books 3, 4 and 5 can be located in Egypt then these Sibyls significantly enrich our understanding of Egyptian Judaism during the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. Collins has suggested that book 3 is unique inasmuch as it looks to a Ptolemaic king as savior figure (the “seventh king of Egypt” vs. 193, see also vss. 318, 608). Barclay, however has warned against making too much of this and suggests that both books 3 and 5 can be seen as popular literature of Alexandrian Judaism. As such they attest to the cultural antagonism between Jews and their Gentile surroundings in that locale. This antagonism would later culminate in the Diaspora Revolt of 115-117 CE. Many of the oracles contain a strong polemic against idol worship and homosexuality, which was a common feature in Jewish apologetic.

Provenance of the Individual Oracles

Locating the date and provenance of the individual books within the collection is extremely difficult. Even books which can be confidently assigned to a particular place and time often contain later interpolations.

Books 1 and 2 are likely a unit and consist of a Jewish oracle which has been edited by a later Christian redactor. In the ψ family of manuscripts book 2 contains a lengthy excerpt from Pseudo-Phocylides, the anonymous 1st century Jewish author whose ethical maxims are usually found embedded in the work of the 6th century BCE philosopher. The prominence given to Phrygia in the book indicates that the work originated in Asia Minor. Since Rome alone is singled out for destruction in the tenth generation and Roman power in Asia Minor was consolidated around 30 BCE, the Jewish sections of the book are likely no earlier than this date. Though there is passing reference to the fall of Jerusalem (1.393-400), Collins has suggested that the brevity of this reference and the fact that Rome is not here singled out for recrimination indicates that this section must be part of the Christian interpolation. Thus the Jewish sections of the book can possibly be dated between 30 BCE and 70 CE [Collins 1983: 331]. The reference to the destruction of the Temple sets the earliest date for the Christian redaction. A terminus ante quem is more difficult to establish.

Books 3 and 5 are widely believed to have originated in Egyptian Jewish circles. Because of references to the seventh king of Egypt (vss. 193, 318, 608), the provenance of most of book 3 can likely be located in Ptolemaic Egypt in the second century BCE. Numerous additions (vss.350-80) s eem to have been made in the first century BCE as is suggested by references to Cleopatra and her anticipated triumph over Rome. Line 776 may be a Christian interpolation inasmuch as it notes that “mortals will invoke the son of the great God.” In his reassessment of the provenance of much of the Jewish Pseudepigrapha, Davila does not wholly refute this consensus but notes that while the work speaks of the Jewish law, the content of this law mostly concerns proper worship of God, and is not concerned with food laws, the Sabbath or circumcision. Thus, while the work could have been authored by an assimilated Jew, it could also be the work of “a gentile who was much taken with and influenced by Judaism in the second or first centuries BCE” (Davila 2005: 186). This is plausible.

The earliest possible date for book 5 is 70 CE, since the work makes use of the Nero Redivivus

motif and thus must come after that emperor’s death in 68 CE. Inasmuch as the work contains positive references to Hadrian (vss. 46-50), the book is likely not later than 132 BCE, since it is difficult to imagine that a Jewish author would have spoken favorably of Hadrian after the Bar Kochba revolt (132-135 BCE). There is a strong anti-Roman sentiment in these oracles, and the Sibyl looks to a heavenly savior figure. This savior figure is identified with Jesus in a Christian interpolation in lines 255-59. Davila suggests that is just as possible that the work is entirely that of a Christ-believing Jew (thus eliminating the need to posit interpolation) or that the work is that of devout gentile God-fearer (Davila 2005: 189).

Book 4 is composite. The original oracle (vss. 49-101) is likely from the Hellenistic period, and there is nothing in the work to suggest Jewish authorship. The oracle has been augmented by a Jewish redactor (vss. 1-48; 102-172). References to the destruction of the temple and to the eruption of Vesuvius date this redaction to the late first century CE. The provenance of the redaction is debated (Thomas 1935; Nikiprowetzky 1970). The work contains a rejection of temple worship (this is in sharp contrast to books 3 and 5) and an interest in baptism. This interest suggests a provenance in Syria or the Jordan Valley, where baptismal movements seem to have been common, but this can not be confirmed (Collins 1983: 382).

Book 6 is not internally presented as a Sibylline Oracle at all but as hymn to Christ. The hymn begins with the baptism of Jesus, ends with his death and suggests that the cross itself was taken up to heaven after the crucifixion. The work must have been written before 300 CE, when it is quoted by Lactantius (Collins 1983: 406). Its provenance is not known.

A terminus ante quem f for book 7 is also provided by Lactantius (DivInst 7.16.13). The work is Christian, and portrays Jesus as a Davidic messiah (vs. 31) who will be enthroned above the angels (vss. 31-33). The work evinces an interest in the baptism of Christ (vss. 65-67) which is to be commemorated by a unique ritual in which a dove is prayed over and then released (vss. 76-81). The provenance of the work is not known.

Book 8 is composite. The first section, vss. 1-216, consists of political prophecies, mostly against Rome. Verses 131-38 were clearly written by a different author than the rest of the work, inasmuch as the pro-Hadrian stance of these verses contradicts verses 50-72. It is uncertain whether this section of the book has its origins amongst a Christian group or a non-Christ believing Jewish group but references to the return of Nero during the reign of Marcus Aurelius (65-74) indicates that book was written during the reign of that emperor, roughly around 175 CE. The second section of the book, lines 217-500, is clearly Christian and is primarily concerned with Christology. It is difficult to date precisely but, again, Lactantius provides a terminus ante quem.

Book 9 is comprised of material in from books 1-8. Book 10 repeats the material in book 4. (See Manuscripts, below).

Books 11-14 seem to represent “an ongoing tradition that was repeatedly updated” (Collins 1983: 430). Each book picks up where the previous one left off and each concludes with a prayer of the Sibyl. Book 11 contains a review of history from the flood to the death of Cleopatra. Several references to Egypt and to the foundation of Alexandria (vs. 219) suggests that the book may have originated in Egypt. Collins suggests that references to Joseph, Moses and Solomon (vss. 29; 38-40; 80-103) indicate that the work is Jewish. Davila, however, does not find this to be persuasive evidence and maintains that the work could just as easily be Christian.

Book 12 shows dependency on SibOr 5, indeed the first eleven verses are taken directly from that book. The bulk of the work is probably Jewish but verses 30-34 and 232, which both speak about the coming Christ (“the secret word of the Most High will come/ wearing flesh like mortals”; 32-33) are Christian interpolations. A reference to the death of the emperor Alexander Severus (288) (235 CE) provides a terminus pro quem of 235 CE.

Book 13 contains praise of Odenath of Palmyra (vss. 150-73) who fought for the Romans against the Parthians during the reign of emperor Gallienus (260-68 CE). Since it does not know of the deaths of either of those figures the work can be dated to approximately 265 CE. The importance accorded Odenath could suggest that the work originated in Syria, but references to Egypt and Alexandria (vss. 43-49) could point to an Egyptian origin. A reference to Decius’ persecution of Christians (vss.87-88) could be a Christian interpolation (Collins 1983: 453) or could indicate that the entire work is Christian (Geffcken 1902: 59-63). Collins suggests that references to the Most High (vs. 109) and the polemic against astrology (vss. 69-73) suggest Jewish authorship, though these elements are also congruent with a Christian provenance.

The dating of book 14 is uncertain. There may be a reference to the Arab conquest (vss. 340-49) which would place the book in the 7th century CE. There are also seem to be references to several Roman emperors, but because the text is exceedingly cryptic, it is difficult identify which ones are being alluded to. There are references to Egypt and to Alexandria (vss. 295-296; 320) which suggests that the book originated there. The concluding verses which proclaim that “the holy nation will hold sway over the whole earth/ for all ages, with their mighty children” (vss. 360-361) suggest Jewish authorship.
details.manuscripts: There are three manuscript groups. Both the φ group and the ψ group contain books 1-8, with the former containing also an anonymous prologue. The φ group begins with book 1 and lacks 8.487-500, while the ψ group begins with book eight (some mss also omit 6 and 7). The third manuscript group, Ω, begins with a ninth book, which is comprised of material in from books 1-8; book 6, then a single verse not found in books 1-8, then 8.218-428. Book 10 repeats the material in book 4. Books 11-14 are preserved only in the Ω group.

details.intro: The *Sibylline Oracles* (Greek: Χρησμοὶ Σιβυλλιακοί / *Chrēsmoi Sibylliakoi*; Latin: *Oracula Sibyllina*) constitute a vast, multifaceted collection of Greek hexameter poems composed by Jewish and early Christian authors between the 2nd century BCE and the 7th century CE. The collection adopts the authoritative literary persona of the **Sibyl**—the inspired, ecstatic prophetess of ancient pagan Greece and Rome (traditionally associated with Erythrae, Cumae, or Delphi)—to proclaim biblical monotheism, castigate pagan idolatry, prophesy the rise and fall of world empires, and announce impending cosmic judgment, divine conflagration (*ekpyrōsis*), and the messianic age.

title: Demetrius the Chronographer — On the Kings in Judaea

details.intro:
Introduction

Demetrius the Chronographer (late 3rd century BCE, ca. 221-204 BCE) is the earliest datable Jewish author writing in Greek whose works have survived. He composed a work entitled On the Kings in Judaea (Περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ βασιλέων) or On the Jews (Περὶ Ἰουδαίων), preserved primarily through excerpts of Alexander Polyhistor quoted in Eusebius's Praeparatio Evangelica (9.19.4; 9.21.1-19; 9.29.1-3, 15, 16) and Clement of Alexandria's Stromateis (1.21.141.1-2).
details.provenance:
Provenance

Alexandria, Egypt, during the reign of Ptolemy IV Philopator (221-204 BCE), as established by Demetrius's own chronological reckonings down to that monarch.

title: Ezekiel the Tragedian — Exagoge (The Exodus Drama)

details.intro: Ezekiel the Tragedian wrote the Exagoge, a Greek tragedy on the exodus in iambic trimeter. Its fragments, preserved by Eusebius from Alexander Polyhistor, include Moses' dream of being enthroned and the description of a phoenix at Elim.
details.provenance: Ezekiel is usually dated to the 2nd c. BCE and probably wrote in Alexandria.

title: Aristobulus of Alexandria — Exegesis of the Law of Moses

details.intro: Aristobulus was a Jewish philosopher who addressed a work on the Torah to a Ptolemaic king. The fragments preserved by Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius explain the Bible's anthropomorphisms allegorically, claim that Greek poets and philosophers borrowed from Moses, and discuss the Sabbath and the date of Passover.
details.provenance: Aristobulus is usually dated to the mid-2nd c. BCE, at Alexandria, in the reign of Ptolemy VI Philometor.

details.intro: The Sentences of Pseudo-Phocylides (CAVT 182 / CANT 35) is a didactic wisdom poem of 230 dactylic hexameters composed in Hellenistic Jewish circles between 100 BCE and 100 CE, combining Mosaic ethical precepts with traditional Greek gnomic form. Edited by Theodor Bergk, Poetae Lyrici Graeci, 4th ed., Vol. 2 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1882), pp. 361-373.
details.manuscripts: Extant in over 150 Byzantine manuscripts, including Mutinensis (M), Vaticanus (Va), Baroccianus (B), and Parisinus 1603 (P), as well as Sibylline Oracles Book 2 (vv. 56-148).

details.intro: The Testament of Orpheus (*Diathēkai* / *Hieroi Logoi*, CAVT 183 / CANT 33) is a Hellenistic Jewish-Orphic poem in dactylic hexameters in which Orpheus recants his former polytheism and instructs Musaeus in the worship of the One True God, explicitly invoking the law of Moses ('the one born of water'). Extant in three recensions: Aristobulus ap. Eusebius (*Praep. Evang.* XIII.12.5), Pseudo-Justin (*Cohortatio ad Graecos* 15; *De Monarchia* 2), and Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata* V.123-125). Edited by Otto Kern, Orphicorum Fragmenta (Berlin, 1922), frr. 245-248.
details.manuscripts: Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica XIII.12; Pseudo-Justin, Cohortatio ad Graecos 15 and De Monarchia 2; Clement of Alexandria, Stromata V.123-125; Theosophia Tubingensis 61.

title: Hellenistic Synagogal Prayers — 16 Synagogal Prayers in Apostolic Constitutions 7-8

details.intro: The *Hellenistic Synagogal Prayers* comprise a collection of sixteen Greek liturgical prayers embedded within the late 4th-century Syrian Christian church order known as the *Apostolic Constitutions* (*Constitutiones Apostolorum*, compiled ca. 380 CE in Antioch or Syria, likely by an Arianizing redactor traditionally associated with Pseudo-Ignatius). Originally identified by Kaufmann Kohler (1893, 1924) and demonstrated systematically by Wilhelm Bousset (1915) and Erwin R. Goodenough (1935), these texts are Greek-language synagogue prayers composed between the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE (ca. 150–300 CE) in the Hellenistic Jewish Diaspora of Syria, Asia Minor, or Egypt. The compiler of the *Apostolic Constitutions* incorporated this existing Jewish liturgical manual into his work, overlaying minimal Christian editorial glosses (typically Christological doxological formulas such as "through Jesus Christ our Lord" at the conclusions):

title: Sentences of the Syriac Menander — Syriac Sapiential Florilegium

details.intro: The *Sentences of the Syriac Menander* (also known as *Pseudo-Menander*, Syriac *Melle d-Menandros*, French *La sagesse de Ménandre l’Égyptien*, German *Die Sprüche des Menanders*) is a Hellenistic Jewish wisdom florilegium of moral instruction and practical aphorisms. Pseudepigraphically attributed to Menander—the renowned 4th-century BCE Athenian comic dramatist whose sententious maxims (*Gnomai Menandrou* / *Menandri Sententiae*) were standard texts in Greco-Roman school curricula—the work was composed originally in Greek between the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, almost certainly in Roman Egypt.

title: Pirke Aboth (Sayings of the Jewish Fathers)

details.intro: The Apocalypse of Sedrach (CAVT 184 / CANT 207) is an eschatological dialogue in which Sedrach (associated with Ezra / Shadrach) intercedes for mankind and questions divine justice regarding the fall of Adam and the punishment of sinners. Edited from Bodleian MS Miscell. gr. 56 by M. R. James, Apocrypha Anecdota (T&S 2.3; Cambridge, 1893), pp. 130-137.
details.manuscripts: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Miscellaneus gr. 56 (15th cent.), fols. 92-100.

details.intro: The Vision of Ezra (Visio Beati Esdrae) is a Latin apocalypse in which Ezra is led by angels through the places of punishment, sees the torments of various classes of sinners and intercedes for them, and is then taken to see the righteous in paradise.
details.provenance: The Latin text is known in a shorter form and in a longer form, which P.-M. Bogaert published from the Teano legendary (Barberini lat. 2318). The work is related to the Greek Apocalypse of Ezra and the Apocalypse of Sedrach; its date is disputed.
